newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Former student leader feels sorry for Deng.
newsitem.headline: Former student leader feels sorry for Deng.

text.p: A prominent student leader in the 1989 Beijing democracy movement, Chai Ling, said she felt sorry for Chinese paramount leader Deng Xioaping, who died on Wednesday.

"I worshipped him very much indeed when I was a youth. After the Tiananmen massacre, I was really shocked and angry and couldn't understand," she said in an interview with Reuters Television on Friday in Boston where she now lives.

"Now after so many years, I understand him better -- his contribution, weakness and tragedy. I feel sorry for him," said the former student leader who fled China for the United States after Beijing's bloody crackdown on the Tiananmen Square protests in 1989.

Chai said Deng misunderstood the motives behind the demonstrations because of his own experience during the ultra-leftist 1966-76 Cultural Revolution when he was purged from the party leadership and forced to perform manual labour.
"Now I understand him. There was no way he could tell the difference between our generation and the Red Guards of those years," she said.
Red Guards were youthful socialist stormtroopers who roamed China during the Cultural Revolution attacking anything seen as tainted by the feudal past or Western influence.
"There was no way he could know people of our generation are totally peaceful, rational, and not violent," she said.

"There was no way he could understand real democracy is different from the 'great democracy' advocated during the Cultural Revolution when violent acts were encouraged. He was limited by his own experience during the Cultural Revolution," she added.
"He was so caught up in his own nightmare, what he suffered in the Cultural Revolution that he could not understand or comprehend his own accomplishments of his reform."
Chai credited Deng's reforms as the impetus for the student demonstrations, saying it was because of his ideas that students could begin to think of protesting.
Deng, credited with bringing communism and capitalism together and transforming China from a backward Stalinist state into an economic powerhouse, ordered the Tiananmen crackdown.
